after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors  $p=⟨0,-1,-{k}^{2}⟩,q=⟨2,4,8⟩$ and $r=⟨-1,-1,5⟩$ are coplanar.
after.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & -{k}^{2} \\ 2 & 4 & 8 \\ -1 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 8 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}|+(-{k}^{2})\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =0+(2\cdot 5-(-1)\cdot 8)-{k}^{2}(2\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 4) \\  & =18-2{k}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =0 \\ 18-2{k}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{k}^{2} & =18 \\ {k}^{2} & =9 \\ k & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-3$ or $k=3.$

after.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(-i+2j-k)-(2i-j) \\  & =-3i+3j-k \\  & =⟨-3,3,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(i+j+2k)-(2i-j) \\  & =-i+2j+2k \\  & =⟨-1,2,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(3i-j+k)-(2i-j) \\  & =i+k \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3(2\cdot 1-0\cdot 2)-3((-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 2)-((-1)\cdot 0-1\cdot 2) \\  & =-6+9+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelpiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|\,5\,|=5.
$$

content.worked_solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(-i+2j-k)-(2i-j) \\  & =-3i+3j-k \\  & =⟨-3,3,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(i+j+2k)-(2i-j) \\  & =-i+2j+2k \\  & =⟨-1,2,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(3i-j+k)-(2i-j) \\  & =i+k \\  & =⟨1,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3(2\cdot 1-0\cdot 2)-3((-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 2)-((-1)\cdot 0-1\cdot 2) \\  & =-6+9+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelpiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|\,5\,|=5.
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨{k}^{2},7,4⟩,$ $b=⟨6,7,4⟩,$ and $c=⟨3,0,2⟩$ are coplanar.
after.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}{k}^{2} & 7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & ={k}^{2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|-7\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|+4\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & ={k}^{2}(7\cdot 2-0\cdot 4)-7(6\cdot 2-3\cdot 4)+4(6\cdot 0-3\cdot 7) \\  & =14{k}^{2}+0-84 \\  & =14{k}^{2}-84 \\  & =14({k}^{2}-6).\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 14({k}^{2}-6) & =0 \\ {k}^{2}-6 & =0 \\ {k}^{2} & =6 \\ k & =\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\sqrt{6}$ or $k=\sqrt{6}.$

content.problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨{k}^{2},7,4⟩,$ $b=⟨6,7,4⟩,$ and $c=⟨3,0,2⟩$ are coplanar.
content.worked_solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}{k}^{2} & 7 & 4 \\ 6 & 7 & 4 \\ 3 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & ={k}^{2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|-7\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|+4\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & ={k}^{2}(7\cdot 2-0\cdot 4)-7(6\cdot 2-3\cdot 4)+4(6\cdot 0-3\cdot 7) \\  & =14{k}^{2}+0-84 \\  & =14{k}^{2}-84 \\  & =14({k}^{2}-6).\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 14({k}^{2}-6) & =0 \\ {k}^{2}-6 & =0 \\ {k}^{2} & =6 \\ k & =\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\sqrt{6}$ or $k=\sqrt{6}.$
